title: Just watched Ingmar Bergman's "Fanny and Alexander" (1984, mini-series version)

commenti.body:
I have no complaints about the long version of this one. It's my favourite movie of all time.

Roger Ebert summed up my reason for loving Fanny och Alexander in the opening and closing paragraph of his write-up in his book 'Great Movies'.

"Ingmar Bergman's "Fanny and Alexander" (1982) was intended to be his last film, and in it, he tends to the business of being young, of being middle-aged, of being old, of being a man, woman, Christian, Jew, sane, crazy, rich, poor, religious, profane. He creates a world in which the utmost certainty exists side by side with ghosts and magic, and a gallery of characters who are unforgettable in their peculiarities. Small wonder one of his inspirations was Dickens.

...At the end, I was subdued and yet exhilarated; something had happened to me that was outside language, that was spiritual, that incorporated Bergman's mysticism; one of his characters suggests that our lives flow into each other's, that even a pebble is an idea of God, that there is a level just out of view where everything really happens."

--- Roger Ebert

I’ve only just finished episode 1 of the long version and I just loved everything about it.  Well, not a fan of fart jokes, but I’ll let it be (silly Germanic people).

Such a rich Christmas dinner party scene.

I first saw the theatrical version as an old soul pre-teen and many years later, after finally becoming older than my soul, I watched the mini-series version. The theatrical is great; most of what's been cut from the miniseries takes place during episodes four and five, mostly from the Ismael and Aron interlude, which I found both profound and bewildering. ItCs been 15 years since I've seen either version; I should watch it again, perhaps during Christmas

Gustav Adolf's christening speech is the conclusion of the story (what follows is an epilogue). But it's not a promise of happiness and harmony to come. He predicts - 

>Soon it will be the hour for robbers and murderers. Evil breaks its chains and runs through the world like a mad dog. The poison effects us all - no-one escapes. 

The story is set in 1907. In just 7 years the Great War will begin, heralding the start of the global catastrophes that characterised the first half of the 20th century. The best years of Fanny and Alexander's lives will be overshadowed by war. All of this is foreshadowed by Gustav Adolf in his speech. 

Such harsh realities are the stuff of Emelie's speech to the actors in ep.2 as she announces her departure from the theatre - 

>I don't bother about myself either. Wars and revolutions and poverty mean nothing to me unless they affect the part I am playing. There are actors who pretend they take an interest in the world, but I know they deceive themselves. I am longing to get away from the theatre. 

Thus begins Emelie's attempt to venture away from the 'little world' and participate in 'reality' - to live selflessly and authentically as a responsible adult and to assume the burden of universal suffering. In episodes 3, 4 and 5, we follow the dismantling of Emelie's naive illusions, as the true nature of 'reality' is revealed to her.

Emelie and the children leave home in order to discover the meaning of home. They leave the theatre in order to discover its true value. Gustav Adolf's speech is a confirmation of these discoveries. 

Where previously Emelie complained of the insular, self indulgent nature of the 'little world' of home, Gustav Adolf celebrates it - 

>It is necessary and not at all shameful to take pleasure in the little world

Gustav Adolf outlines the value and, indeed, the *necessity* of the little world, demonstrating a depth of character and insight we had not previously granted this rather buffoonish philanderer. He is careful to include the actors in this world, telling them - 

>it is you who are to give us our supernatural shudders and still more mundane amusements

What follows this speech, in the story's epilogue, is just that - *mundane amusements and supernatural shudders.* The domestic comedy - the trivial but nonetheless enjoyable stuff of popular theatre - continues. Gustav Adolf continues to torment the maid, Maj, with his stubborn generosity. Carl and Lydia are still trapped in the archetypal unhappy marriage, tragic in one moment, comic in the next. The malevolent ghost of the Bishop walks the hallways. This *is* a vindication of Gustav Adolf's speech. These mundane amusements and supernatural shudders *are* the 'little world' he finds so necessary.
Thanks for the correction and analysis!
It's only my interpretation! There are many!
